title: Embedding-Space Fingerprinting of LoRA Fine-Tunes: Recovering the Training-Data Domain from the Model Artifact Alone
content:
Computer Science > Artificial Intelligence
  [Submitted on 5 Nov 2026]
Title:Embedding-Space Fingerprinting of LoRA Fine-Tunes: Recovering the Training-Data Domain from the Model Artifact Alone
View PDF HTML (experimental)
            Abstract:When a base language model is fine-tuned with Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA), how much of the training data domain leaks into the resulting artifact? This paper studies whether a simple classifier can recover the domain of a fine-tune given only the model artifact (weight deltas, internal activations on a fixed probe set, or generated text) without ever observing the training data. Using one base model (Qwen3.5-0.8B), 36 LoRA fine-tunes are produced over 18 public datasets in five domains (medical, code, mathematics, non-English text, narrative prose), and three feature families are extracted at decreasing levels of access: white-box weights, gray-box activations, and black-box outputs. A leave-one-dataset-out (LODO) protocol, frozen before any result was seen, tests whether the domain of a fine-tune trained on a previously unseen dataset can be identified. The domain is recoverable well above chance (20%) from gray-box activations (61%) and black-box outputs (64%); white-box weight statistics reach 42%. Contrary to the pre-registered hypothesis that signal decays monotonically from weights to activations to outputs, activations and outputs were more informative than the weight-delta statistics. The black-box result holds unchanged (64%) when only generated text is used, without token probabilities. Domain accuracy is also stable when a third run per dataset is trained on an independently drawn data subsample, and black-box predictions are unaffected by the LoRA rank (8-64). All code and per-run feature vectors are released.

report.summary: Researchers show LoRA fine-tunes leak their training-data domain, identifying it from generated text alone at 64% accuracy—better than weight statistics.
report.background: LoRA has become a default way to cheaply adapt open language models, and fine-tuned adapters are routinely shared on model hubs or exposed through hosted APIs. That raises a practical question: when a LoRA artifact is published, how much can it reveal about the data used to train it? Prior work on model privacy has focused on membership inference, data extraction, and watermarking, but domain-level leakage is less understood. The paper tests whether the training-data domain—medical, code, math, non-English text, or narrative prose—can be inferred from the artifact alone, without access to the original dataset. The result matters for open-weight distribution, data provenance, compliance reviews, and privacy auditing because LoRA’s low-rank updates are often assumed to be compact and relatively opaque.
key_points: The study trains 36 LoRA adapters on one Qwen3.5-0.8B base model, covering 18 public datasets across five domains. It compares three access levels: white-box weight deltas, gray-box internal activations, and black-box generated outputs, using a pre-registered leave-one-dataset-out test.

Domain recovery is well above the 20% chance level: black-box outputs reach 64%, gray-box activations 61%, and white-box weight statistics only 42%. This contradicts the expected pattern that signal would decay from weights to activations to outputs.

The black-box result is especially practical: it holds at 64% using only generated text, without token probabilities. Accuracy stays stable when a third independent data subsample is used and when LoRA rank varies from 8 to 64.

The authors release code and per-run feature vectors, making the work reproducible. The findings suggest even simple classifiers can fingerprint a fine-tune’s domain, so LoRA artifacts should not be treated as domain-neutral by default.
report.impact: For the AI industry, the paper adds a new privacy and provenance concern to model sharing: LoRA adapters can disclose the kind of data used to build them even when the original data is withheld. Model hubs, auditors, and compliance teams may need domain-leakage checks before publishing adapters or exposing fine-tuned APIs. For developers, the result means LoRA is not an anonymization layer; sensitive-domain fine-tunes may need sanitization, differential privacy, access controls, or deliberate output monitoring. For regular users, the upside is better provenance and trust signals for public models, but the downside is that domain inference can expose sensitive specialization—for example, a medical or legal adapter—without direct data access. The black-box result is particularly relevant because it requires only generated text, the same surface most users and APIs already see.
report.tools: Start with Hugging Face PEFT and adapter-transformers for creating and inspecting LoRA artifacts, plus Transformers for activation extraction. Captum or LIT can help with probing and interpretability, while ML Privacy Meter and OpenDP are useful for privacy auditing and differential-privacy fine-tuning. The paper’s released code and per-run feature vectors are the most direct way to reproduce or extend the fingerprinting pipeline.
